title: When Kidneys Cannot Clear the Salt

scenes.tts: A seabird takes in seawater, or a heavy load of salt. Seawater is near one thousand milliosmoles per kilogram, an approximate figure. That counts dissolved particles in each kilogram of water. Bird kidneys cannot make urine as salty as the sea. So where does the extra salt go?

scenes.visual: Sea bar, bird block with a kidneys chip and a urine arrow; salt arrow in from the sea; a red question-mark route appears.
scenes.narration: A seabird takes in seawater, or a heavy load of salt. Seawater is near 1,000 mOsm/kg, an approximate figure. That counts dissolved particles in each kilogram of water. Bird kidneys cannot make urine as salty as the sea. So where does the extra salt go?

scenes.tts: Marine birds such as cormorants and gulls often feed at sea, where fresh water is scarce. Think about the kidney route alone. A bird that cleared the salt of seawater through its kidneys alone would need more water than it drank. The kidney route alone leaves the bird short of water.
scenes.visual: Chain gulp, kidneys, less salty urine; two bars appear: water drunk, and a taller red bar for water needed by kidneys alone.
scenes.narration: Marine birds such as cormorants and gulls often feed at sea, where fresh water is scarce. Think about the kidney route alone. A bird that cleared the salt of seawater through its kidneys alone would need more water than it drank. The kidney route alone leaves the bird short of water.

scenes.tts: In 1958, Knut Schmidt-Nielsen, C B Jorgensen and H Osaki tested whether another route existed. They gave double-crested cormorants a load of salt, by mouth or by infusion. Then they collected two fluids. One was the cloacal fluid, urine mixed with feces. The other was a clear fluid that dripped from the beak. Paired nasal salt glands above the eyes made it.
scenes.caption: In 1958, Knut Schmidt-Nielsen, C. B. Jørgensen and H. Osaki tested whether another route existed. They gave double-crested cormorants a load of salt, by mouth or by infusion. Then they collected two fluids. One was the cloacal fluid, urine mixed with feces. The other was a clear fluid that dripped from the beak. Paired nasal salt glands above the eyes made it.
scenes.visual: Salt load goes into a cormorant block; nasal glands send a green arrow to one vial, kidneys an orange arrow to a second vial.
scenes.narration: In 1958, Knut Schmidt-Nielsen, C. B. Jørgensen and H. Osaki tested whether another route existed. They gave double-crested cormorants a load of salt, by mouth or by infusion. Then they collected two fluids. One was the cloacal fluid, urine mixed with feces. The other was a clear fluid that dripped from the beak. Paired nasal salt glands above the eyes made it.

scenes.tts: If these birds handled salt the way mammals do, the cloacal fluid would carry the load. It did not. After the load, the nasal fluid held about five hundred to six hundred millimoles per litre of sodium chloride. That is similar to seawater, or somewhat above it. The glands put out about ten times as much salt as the cloaca.
scenes.caption: If these birds handled salt the way mammals do, the cloacal fluid would carry the load. It did not. After the load, the nasal fluid held about 500 to 600 mmol/L of sodium chloride. That is similar to seawater, or somewhat above it. The glands put out about ten times as much salt as the cloaca.
scenes.visual: Bar chart: nasal fluid NaCl 500 to 600 band against seawater sodium about 470; then a 10 to 1 pair of salt output bars.
scenes.narration: If these birds handled salt the way mammals do, the cloacal fluid would carry the load. It did not. After the load, the nasal fluid held about 500 to 600 mmol/L of sodium chloride. That is similar to seawater, or somewhat above it. The glands put out about ten times as much salt as the cloaca.

scenes.tts: A gland that excretes salt more concentrated than seawater changes the water budget. A bird can get rid of the salt of a gulp of seawater in less water than the gulp held. It keeps the difference. Gulls reach even higher values than these cormorants did.
scenes.visual: Gulp box with a salt chip goes through the gland into a shorter gland-fluid box with the same salt chip, and a blue block for the water kept.
scenes.narration: A gland that excretes salt more concentrated than seawater changes the water budget. A bird can get rid of the salt of a gulp of seawater in less water than the gulp held. It keeps the difference. Gulls reach even higher values than these cormorants did.

scenes.tts: What did the experiment show? It ruled in a route outside the kidneys, through which these birds can excrete a salt load. It did not show how the gland concentrates salt. It did not show that every bird has active salt glands. Sea turtles and the marine iguana have salt glands too. In cormorants, salt can leave by a route besides the kidneys.
scenes.visual: Two-route bird block; green route confirmed, red question marks on how and on every bird, marine reptiles chip.
